course: Daily Egg Sales: Layer Flock System
module_title: From Point of Lay to Peak

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: Point of lay is when your pullets start laying eggs, usually around 18 to 20 weeks old. This is the moment you've been waiting forâyour first eggs and your first income. But it's also a critical transition. The birds are still growing while starting to lay, so their bodies are under stress. If you manage them poorly now, they may never reach peak production, and you'll lose money. Peak production for most layer breeds in Africa (like Isa Brown, Lohmann, or local improved breeds) is around 90% layâthat means 9 eggs per 10 hens per day. That peak usually comes at 28 to 32 weeks of age. Your goal in this module is to get your flock from point of lay to that peak as quickly and smoothly as possible, and then hold it there. Why does it matter? Because a hen that starts laying well and reaches peak will give you 300 to 320 eggs in her first year. A hen that is poorly managed might give you only 200. That difference of 100 eggs per hen, at say 300 shillings per egg in your local market, is 30,000 shillings per hen per year. For a flock of 100 hens, that's 3 million shillings lost. So the steps you take in the next few weeks directly determine your profit. In this module, you'll learn exactly what to do: how to feed, water, light, and handle your birds to push them to peak. You'll also learn common mistakes that keep African farmers stuck at 50% lay, and how to fix them. By the end, you'll have a practical plan to get your flock to 90% lay and keep it there for months.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To manage your flock from point of lay to peak, you need a few basic tools and materials. Most are cheap and available in local agro-vet shops or markets. First, you need a reliable feed supply. Layer mash or pellets with 16-18% protein and 3.5-4.5% calcium are essential. In many African countries, you can buy commercial layer feed from companies like Ugachick in Uganda, Kenchic in Kenya, or similar. If you mix your own feed, you'll need maize, soybean meal, fish meal, limestone, and a mineral premix. A simple kitchen scale or a feed scoop that holds exactly 1 kg will help you measure daily ration. Second, you need clean water. A 20-litre bucket or a plastic drinker is fine. For 100 hens, provide at least 2 drinkers and 2 feeders to avoid crowding. Third, lighting. If your hens are indoors and daylight is less than 14 hours, you need a bulb (LED or fluorescent) and a timer or a person to switch it on and off. A simple 40-watt bulb per 20 square meters is enough. Fourth, a thermometer to check coop temperatureâideally 18-24Â°C. Fifth, a record book or notebook to track daily egg count, feed intake, and any deaths. Sixth, gloves and boots for cleaning. Seventh, a disinfectant like Virkon or bleach for cleaning drinkers and feeders. Finally, a small first-aid kit with antibiotics, vitamins, and dewormers. You don't need expensive equipment. Many successful farmers use locally made feeders from old plastic containers and drinkers from cut jerrycans. The key is consistency and cleanliness. Make sure you have these items before your pullets start laying, so you're not caught unprepared. A good practice is to stock up on feed for at least two weeks, so you never run out.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps to move your flock from point of lay to peak production. Step 1: Prepare the coop. Clean and disinfect the laying house at least one week before you expect the first eggs. Provide one nest box for every 5 hens, filled with soft bedding like wood shavings or dry grass. Make sure the coop is well-ventilated but not drafty. Step 2: Adjust feed. Switch from grower feed to layer feed gradually over 7 days. Start with 25% layer feed mixed with 75% grower, then increase every two days. By day 7, they should be on 100% layer feed. Give each hen about 110-120 grams of feed per day. For 100 hens, that's 11-12 kg per day. Split into two feedings: morning and afternoon. Step 3: Provide clean water at all times. A laying hen drinks about 200-250 ml per day. In hot weather, they drink more. Never let drinkers go empty. Step 4: Manage lighting. Hens need 14-16 hours of light per day to lay well. If natural daylight is less, use artificial light. For example, if sunrise is 6:30 am and sunset is 6:30 pm, that's 12 hours. You need 2-4 more hours. Turn on lights at 5:00 am and off at 7:00 am, then on again from 6:00 pm to 8:00 pm. Use a timer to keep it consistent. Step 5: Collect eggs at least twice a dayâmorning and evening. This prevents eggs from being broken or eaten. Step 6: Monitor weight and health. Weigh a few hens weekly. They should gain about 100-150 grams per week until 30 weeks. Watch for signs of disease: pale combs, ruffled feathers, or drop in feed intake. Step 7: Record everything. Write down daily egg count, feed used, and any problems. At peak, you should see 90 eggs per 100 hens. If you're below 70%, check your feeding, lighting, and water. Step 8: Keep stress low. Avoid moving birds, loud noises, or introducing new birds. Stress can drop production by 10-20% quickly. Follow these steps consistently, and your flock should reach peak by 30 weeks.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Many farmers fail to reach peak production because of avoidable mistakes. Here are the most common ones and how to fix them. Mistake 1: Feeding too little or wrong feed. Some farmers continue with grower feed or give kitchen scraps only. This leads to low protein and calcium, so hens lay small eggs or stop laying. Fix: Use commercial layer feed with 16-18% protein and 4% calcium. If mixing your own, ensure correct ratios. Give 110-120g per hen daily. Mistake 2: Not enough water. A hen without water for even a few hours can stop laying for days. Fix: Provide at least 2 drinkers per 100 hens and check them twice daily. Clean drinkers with bleach solution once a week. Mistake 3: Poor lighting. In many African regions, daylight is 12 hours year-round. Without extra light, hens may lay at 50-60% instead of 90%. Fix: Add artificial light to reach 14-16 hours total. Use a timer to avoid forgetting. Mistake 4: Overcrowding. More than 5 hens per square meter causes stress and disease. Fix: Provide at least 0.2 square meters per hen in the coop, and 0.5 square meters in the run. Mistake 5: Dirty nest boxes. Eggs get dirty or broken, and hens may eat eggs. Fix: Clean nest boxes daily, replace bedding weekly, and collect eggs at least twice a day. Mistake 6: Sudden changes. Changing feed brand, moving the flock, or adding new birds can cause a drop in lay. Fix: Make changes gradually over a week. Mistake 7: Ignoring parasites. Worms and mites reduce egg production. Fix: Deworm every 3 months and treat mites with dust or spray. Mistake 8: Not recording. Without records, you can't tell if production is dropping. Fix: Keep a simple notebook. Write down daily egg count and feed intake. If you see a drop, act immediately. By avoiding these mistakes, you'll reach peak faster and keep it longer.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Safety and best practice protect both you and your hens. Start with personal safety. Always wear gloves and boots when cleaning the coop or handling sick birds. Chicken manure can carry bacteria like Salmonella. Wash your hands with soap after any contact. If you use chemicals like disinfectants or insecticides, follow the instructions and keep them away from feed and water. For the hens, biosecurity is key. Keep visitors out of the coop unless necessary. If you must enter, use footbaths with disinfectant. Never bring in new birds without a 2-week quarantine. This prevents diseases like Newcastle or avian flu from wiping out your flock. Clean drinkers and feeders daily with clean water. Once a week, scrub them with a mild bleach solution (1 tablespoon per 4 litres) and rinse well. Replace bedding in nest boxes weekly. Collect eggs promptly and store them in a cool place. Best practice for peak production includes: consistent routine. Feed, water, and light at the same times every day. Hens are creatures of habit. Any change stresses them. Keep temperature stable. If it's too hot (above 30Â°C), hens eat less and lay fewer eggs. Provide shade, ventilation, and cool water. If it's too cold, add bedding and block drafts. Handle hens gently. Rough handling can cause injuries or stress. When you need to catch a hen, do it at night when they are calm. Use a net or hold them by the body, not the wings or neck. Provide a balanced diet. Besides layer feed, you can give small amounts of greens like kale or amaranth for vitamins, and crushed oyster shells for extra calcium. But don't overdo scrapsâthey dilute the feed. Finally, keep records. This is a safety tool: if you see a drop in production or feed intake, you can catch disease early. A simple notebook with daily egg count, deaths, and any symptoms is enough. By following these practices, you'll have a healthy flock and a profitable egg business.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now it's time to put what you've learned into practice. This exercise will help you plan and manage your flock from point of lay to peak. Follow these steps and record your results. Step 1: Assess your current situation. If your pullets are not yet laying, note their age. If they are already laying, note the current lay percentage. Count your hens and calculate: (number of eggs collected yesterday Ã· number of hens) Ã 100. For example, 60 eggs from 100 hens = 60% lay. Step 2: Check your feed. Look at the label on your feed bag. It should say 16-18% protein and 3.5-4.5% calcium. If not, buy proper layer feed. Weigh out 110g per hen for one day. For 100 hens, that's 11 kg. Split into two feedings. Step 3: Check water. Ensure you have at least 2 drinkers per 100 hens. Fill them with clean water. Add a vitamin supplement if birds are stressed. Step 4: Check lighting. Count the hours of natural daylight in your area. If it's less than 14 hours, plan to add artificial light. For example, if daylight is 12 hours, add 2 hours in the morning (5-7 am) and 2 hours in the evening (6-8 pm). Use a timer or set an alarm. Step 5: Clean and prepare nest boxes. Provide one nest box per 5 hens. Fill with soft bedding. Collect eggs twice daily. Step 6: Keep records for one week. Use a notebook to write down daily: date, number of eggs, feed given (kg), water checked (yes/no), and any deaths or sick birds. Step 7: Calculate your weekly lay percentage. At the end of the week, total eggs divided by (hens Ã 7) Ã 100. If you're below 70%, review your feeding, lighting, and water. Step 8: Set a goal. Aim for 90% lay by 30 weeks of age. If your hens are already 30 weeks and below 80%, identify the weakest area and fix it. Repeat this exercise every week until you reach peak. Share your results with a fellow farmer for accountability. This hands-on practice will build your skills and confidence.

quiz.q: At what age do pullets typically start laying eggs?
quiz.explanation: Point of lay for most layer breeds is around 18-20 weeks.

quiz.q: What is considered peak production for a layer flock?
quiz.explanation: Peak production is typically around 90% lay, meaning 9 eggs per 10 hens per day.

quiz.q: How many eggs can a well-managed hen produce in her first year?
quiz.explanation: A hen that reaches peak and is well-managed can produce 300-320 eggs in the first year.

quiz.q: What protein percentage should layer feed contain?
quiz.explanation: Layer feed should have 16-18% protein to support egg production.

quiz.q: How much feed should each laying hen receive per day?
quiz.explanation: A laying hen needs about 110-120 grams of feed per day.

quiz.q: How many hours of light per day do laying hens need for good production?
quiz.explanation: Hens need 14-16 hours of light daily to lay well.

quiz.q: What is the recommended number of nest boxes for 100 hens?
quiz.explanation: Provide one nest box for every 5 hens, so 20 boxes for 100 hens.

quiz.q: How often should you collect eggs?
quiz.explanation: Collect eggs at least twice daily to prevent breakage and egg eating.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake that leads to low egg production?
options: D) Collecting eggs twice a day
quiz.explanation: Insufficient light is a major cause of low lay in many African regions.

quiz.q: How should you switch from grower to layer feed?
quiz.explanation: Gradual transition over 7 days prevents digestive upset.

quiz.q: What is the ideal calcium percentage in layer feed?
quiz.explanation: Layer feed should have 3.5-4.5% calcium for strong eggshells.

quiz.q: What should you do if your flock's lay drops suddenly?
options: B) Check feed, water, and lighting
quiz.explanation: A sudden drop usually indicates a problem with feed, water, light, or disease.

quiz.q: How much water does a laying hen drink per day?
quiz.explanation: A laying hen drinks about 200-250 ml of water daily.

quiz.q: Why is overcrowding bad for laying hens?
options: A) It causes stress and disease
quiz.explanation: Overcrowding stresses hens and spreads disease, lowering production.

quiz.q: What is biosecurity?
options: B) Measures to prevent disease entry
quiz.explanation: Biosecurity includes practices like footbaths and quarantine to keep diseases out.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm your flock?
quiz.explanation: Deworming every 3 months helps control internal parasites.

quiz.q: What should you do with new birds before adding them to the flock?
quiz.explanation: Quarantine new birds for 2 weeks to prevent disease spread.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for laying hens?
quiz.explanation: Hens lay best when temperatures are between 18-24Â°C.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important?
options: B) To track production and spot problems
quiz.explanation: Records help you monitor performance and detect issues early.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see a hen with a pale comb and ruffled feathers?
options: B) Isolate and check for disease
quiz.explanation: These are signs of illness; isolate the bird and seek treatment.

quiz.q: How can you provide extra calcium to laying hens?
quiz.explanation: Crushed oyster shells are a good source of additional calcium.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of artificial lighting?
options: B) To increase daylight hours to 14-16
quiz.explanation: Artificial light extends daylight to 14-16 hours, stimulating laying.

quiz.q: What is a sign of stress in laying hens?
quiz.explanation: Stress often causes a drop in egg production.

quiz.q: How often should you clean drinkers and feeders?
quiz.explanation: Clean drinkers and feeders daily to prevent disease.

quiz.q: What is the recommended space per hen in the coop?
quiz.explanation: Provide at least 0.2 square meters per hen in the coop.

quiz.q: What should you do before your pullets start laying?
options: B) Clean and disinfect the coop
quiz.explanation: Clean and disinfect the coop one week before expected lay.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of splitting feed into two meals?
options: A) Reduces waste and improves digestion
quiz.explanation: Two feedings reduce waste and help hens digest better.

quiz.q: What should you do if your flock is at 60% lay at 30 weeks?
options: B) Review and fix feeding, lighting, water
quiz.explanation: At 30 weeks, you should be near peak; low lay indicates a management issue.

quiz.q: Why is it important to handle hens gently?
options: A) To avoid stress and injury
B) To make them lay more eggs
D) To prevent them from flying
quiz.explanation: Gentle handling reduces stress, which can lower egg production.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for biosecurity?
options: A) Allow visitors into the coop
D) Bring in new birds often
quiz.explanation: Footbaths help prevent disease from entering the coop.
